newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian nurses, teachers protest over layoffs.
newsitem.headline: Romanian nurses, teachers protest over layoffs.

text.p: Health and education workers marched through Bucharest on Monday to denounce job cuts imposed by Romania's new centrist government in two sectors long plagued by low pay and official neglect.

"Thieves! Thieves! Health! Health!" the 3,000 protesters shouted in protest against average monthly wages equivalent to $70 per month -- even less than the average pay of $80 since introduction in February of economic reforms.
Determined to end seven years of sluggish post-communist reform, the government has freed prices of staples and utilities, curtailed subsidies and passed an austerity budget.
The Health and Education Ministries last week announced job cuts of nearly 10 percent among the country's 300,000 health workers and 450,000 teaching staff.
"We have nothing against reform and restructuring. State employees must take their share of the burden," Marius Petcu, leader of the Sanitas trade union federation, told Reuters.

"But we cannot agree with reforms that start by sacking one in 10 of our people while the health system is on the brink of collapse. Reform should start by attracting nurses to places where old people walk several kilometres to see one."

Poverty, malnutrition and poor hygiene have reduced life expectancy and led to a return of illnesses like viral meningitis, typhoid and cholera. Tuberculosis, cancer and venereal diseases are on the rise and the country is afflicted by 54 percent of Europe's juvenile AIDS cases.

Romania's health care system, its principle of free medicine for all exposed as a sham under communist rule, has virtually collapsed since 1989 through misuse of funds, bad management and lack of medicines and equipment.

The centrists, who defeated ex-communists in last November's election, have adopted a health insurance bill setting up Western-style social security contributions by linking pay to the number of patients treated.

Education is also in a desperate state, with teachers already leaving the profession en masse. Trade unions say 300 of Romania's 27,000 kindergardens and schools have no electricity and a further 160 no heating.
Corneliu Caranica, leader of one of the country's education unions, said the education system needed reforming, "but in content, not in staff numbers. Layoffs don't bring efficiency."
